concept.name: Option exercise
concept.definition: The act by which the holder of an option invokes the contractual right to buy (call) or sell (put) the underlying at the strike price, converting the option position into a transaction or position in the underlying.
concept.intuition: Exercising is cashing in the ticket: instead of selling the option, you use it to force the trade at the strike.
concept.mechanics: The holder gives irrevocable exercise instructions to their broker, which routes them to the clearing organization (OCC for U.S. securities options) before exercise cut-off times; settlement then proceeds as a purchase or sale of the underlying (physical) or a cash payment. At expiration, OCC's 'exercise by exception' automatically exercises options in-the-money by at least $0.01 unless contrary instructions are submitted. Exercising early forfeits remaining time value, so holders often prefer selling the option.
concept.failure_modes: Exercise requires the cash or stock to complete the underlying transaction; holders without it may be restricted by their broker. Failing to submit explicit instructions around thresholds or after-hours price moves can produce unintended exercises or lapses of in-the-money value.
concept.misconceptions: Exercise is not the usual way to realize an option's value — most long options are closed by sale (historically roughly 70% of contracts are closed out and only a small share are exercised), because selling preserves time value that exercise destroys.
concept.example: Exercising an OICX 60 call means buying 100 shares at $60 each; if the stock is $68 and the call trades at $8.50, selling the call realizes $8.50 while exercise-plus-sale realizes only the $8 intrinsic value.
